alternatives: Bind the route to Daemon.start(): rejected, it throws on a second call and cannot express idempotency.
Let start force a parked run back to running: rejected, it would race the quota scheduler's own resume and discard the journaled countdown target.
payload.decision: The start control never creates a process or a Run. Spec 021 B-2 fixes the boot order (lock, journals, recovery, then the loop and this API), so by the time an HTTP request can arrive the daemon is already up, and process lifecycle belongs to spec 023's daemon start|stop|status. Within a hosted daemon, start delegates to resume when the run is paused, is an idempotent no-op returning applied:false when the run is already running, and is refused with a conflict when the run is parked, completed, or failed. A journal with no run at all is also a conflict.
payload.rationale: B-5 lists start alongside pause and resume as a run-level control and asks for idempotency where the verb implies it, but the Daemon's own start() is a one-shot process bootstrap that throws when called twice, so binding the route to it would make the first POST work and every later one an error. Parked is the quota scheduler's state to leave (spec 015 B-3 resumes it on its own countdown) and completed/failed are terminal sinks in spec 013's transition table, so a control verb that claimed to leave them would be inventing an edge the state machine does not have.
payload.title: POST /api/run/start means "ensure the run is running", not "boot a daemon"

alternatives: Have the ControlTarget methods return the record: rejected, it would change spec 021's Daemon signatures from this spec's territory.
payload.decision: A control handler snapshots the journal record count, invokes the daemon's own control method, and returns the first record appended by that call whose kind starts with "control." (falling back to the first appended record). The API appends nothing to either chain. An idempotent no-op returns applied:false with record:null rather than a synthesized record.
payload.rationale: B-5 requires controls to return the journaled control record and B-6 requires the API to serve only journal-derived state. Having the API write its own control record would give two writers for one fact and would let a response describe something the daemon never queued; diffing the journal keeps the daemon the single author of the record and makes the response literally a read of what was written.
payload.title: The control record a control endpoint returns is diffed out of the journal, never written by the API

alternatives: Serve raw bytes only: rejected, it breaks the one-envelope rule and the typed client.
Serve the envelope only: rejected, the web UI would have to base64-decode every screenshot in JavaScript to display it.
payload.decision: GET /api/evidence/<hash> answers {ok:true,data:{hash,mediaType,bytes,text,base64}} like every other read route; text evidence fills text and png evidence fills base64, with the other field explicitly null. The same URL with ?raw=1 serves the file bytes with its own content type. The hash must match 64 lowercase hex characters, so no path can be traversed and no file outside the evidence directory is reachable.
payload.rationale: AC-2 requires every read endpoint to return the documented envelope, which a bare image body would not, and the typed client can only cover a route that answers in the envelope. Spec 024 B-5 nonetheless needs a URL an can load directly, which the envelope cannot provide, so the raw form exists as a narrow, read-only, content-addressed affordance rather than as a second response shape for the documented route.
payload.title: Evidence is served in the standard envelope, with ?raw=1 for the bytes

alternatives: Truncate long strings in place: rejected, a silently shortened stderr tail reads as the whole tail.
Raise the ring capacity: rejected, B-4 fixes it at 256 and the problem is per-event size, not count.
payload.decision: SSE event data is the journal record's payload verbatim while its JSON encoding is at most 4096 characters. Past that the event carries {bounded:true, seq, kind, chars} instead, and the client refetches the derived state from the read routes. Quota ticks are synthesized on their own 15 s cadence while the run is parked, computed from the journaled target each time.
payload.rationale: B-4 asks for bounded session stream summaries, and session.result payloads carry a 16 KB stderr tail that would dominate the 256-event ring and shrink the replay window to almost nothing. Truncating the strings inside a payload would produce an event that looks complete and is not, which is exactly what B-6 forbids; naming the seq and the real size is the honest bound, and the full record is still reachable through the read routes.
payload.title: An oversized event payload is replaced by a size marker, never truncated in place

alternatives: Report the registry's raw answer: rejected, the UI would show the daemon about to redo work it already did.
payload.decision: Before computing nextReady, the DAG view overrides the registry implementation field of every spec the journal shows shipped (to orchestrator-shipped) or an operator has skipped through a control (to orchestrator-skipped), exactly as the daemon's own loop does. Each node still reports the registry's raw implementation value, plus a skipped flag, so nothing about the registry is hidden.
payload.rationale: The target repo's registry only flips a spec to non-pending once the build session's frontmatter edit is merged and re-read, so between shipping a spec and that flip landing, an unmasked nextReady answers with a spec the daemon has demonstrably finished. B-6 forbids the API disagreeing with a fold of the journal, and the journal is the side that knows the spec shipped.

alternatives: Let the error propagate: rejected, one missing file would take down the whole view.
Treat an unreadable file as drifted: rejected, it fabricates a cascade from an I/O error.
payload.decision: Pins are read once per request and memoized. A read failure sets the node's currentPin to null and fills pinError with the reason; the lookup handed to invalidatedSet and nextReady falls back to the pin recorded when that spec shipped, so the invalidation cascade never fires on the strength of an I/O error.
payload.rationale: dag.ts's pinOf throws on an unreadable spec.md, which would turn one missing file into a 500 for the whole DAG view; returning an empty or sentinel pin instead would make the spec look drifted and cascade an invalidation across every dependent (spec 012 B-4). Reporting the read failure as a read failure is the only answer that is neither a crash nor a false claim about drift.
payload.title: A spec file that cannot be read is a pin error, never pin drift

alternatives: Add an append listener to journal.ts: rejected, it edits spec 011's territory from this spec's session.
Watch the journal file with fs.watch: rejected, it would reimplement the record parsing journal.ts already owns.
payload.decision: A pump reads the same JournalView the GET routes fold, on a 250 ms interval, and publishes one event per record whose seq it has not seen. It starts from the journal's current tail, so opening a stream does not replay the whole run as if it were happening now. The API is handed a view over the daemon's live handle (journalViewFromHandle) and never opens a second writer.
payload.rationale: B-4 asks for a subscription to journal appends, but journal.ts (spec 011's territory) has no listener seam, and adding one from this spec's territory would edit an owning spec's file. Polling a view of the same handle keeps the stream a strict projection of what is durably on disk, which is what B-6 needs anyway: nothing can be announced over SSE that a later fold would deny.
payload.title: The event stream polls a read-only journal view rather than subscribing to appends

alternatives: Emit the client from a schema at build time: rejected, the repo deliberately has no build step.
Reject unknown spec ids at the control route: rejected, it couples every control to a subprocess read.
Require X-Api-Version on every request: rejected, AC-2 exercises the API through curl.
payload.decision: The client is hand-written but takes every path from the shared API_ROUTES table and every payload type from types.ts, so a route or shape cannot drift between server and client without failing typecheck. Control endpoints validate a spec id by shape (a leading alphanumeric followed by alphanumerics, dot, underscore, or hyphen) and do not check registry membership. apiVersion gating is opt-in: a request that declares X-Api-Version is held to it, one that declares nothing is served on the v1 assumption.
payload.rationale: FR-002 asks for a generated typed client; the property that matters is a single source of truth, which a shared route table and shared types give without adding a codegen step to a repo that has no build step. Validating a spec id against the registry would make every control depend on a spec-spine subprocess succeeding, so a control could fail for a reason unrelated to the control. Requiring a version header would break plain curl, which AC-2 makes a first-class client.
payload.title: api-client.ts is route-table driven rather than code-generated, and spec ids are shape-validated only

alternatives: Treat a refreshed pin as ordinary drift and let the invalidation cascade fire, which would have made the API contradict the scheduler it reports on.

Have the API recompute re-adoption from the registry the way the daemon does, which would require it to append dag.adopted.refreshed records and break D-2's rule that this module is never an author of journal facts.
payload.decision: shippedMapFromJournal seeds from the first (immutable) dag.adopted record and then replays every dag.adopted.refreshed record in journal order, applying {id, newPin} as an adopted entry, exactly as the daemon's own computeShippedMap does. The API still appends nothing: it replays only what the daemon already journaled, and never performs the daemon's re-adoption write itself, so it reports the shipped-set as of the last thing the daemon committed.
payload.rationale: Spec 021 D-11 (continuous adoption tracking) landed on the default branch after this spec's implementation was written, and it moved re-adoption out of the immutable dag.adopted record into its own dag.adopted.refreshed record. A fold that stopped at dag.adopted reported the superseded pin for every re-adopted spec, which made the node read drifted, put it in invalidatedSet, and cascaded 'dependency is invalidated (pin drift)' across all of its dependents. /api/dag would then answer nextReady: null and show the whole backlog stalled while the daemon was demonstrably still building, which is precisely the cached-status-that-disagrees-with-a-fold that B-6 forbids. Two regression tests in state.test.ts pin both the fold and the resulting DAG view.
payload.title: The API's shipped-map fold replays dag.adopted.refreshed, so /api/dag agrees with the daemon's scheduler

alternatives: status = /api/run only: rejected, the human rendering would show quota state the --json form omitted.
A CLI-local StatusView type: rejected, it would be a second copy of the wire contract living outside spec 022's territory.
payload.decision: orchestrator status fetches /api/run and /api/quota and renders them together; with --json it prints {ok:true,data:{run,quota}} composed from the two served envelopes, whose payloads are the RunView and QuotaView types verbatim from the API's own types.ts. Every other API-backed command maps to exactly one route and prints that route's envelope unchanged.
payload.rationale: B-3 requires human output to state a quota horizon as an estimate when the daemon says it is estimated, and a run view alone cannot do that: a parked run reads as idle. Composing two shapes that are both already shared with the server introduces no third declaration of the contract, so a change to either shape still fails typecheck here rather than surfacing at runtime.
payload.title: status composes run and quota; every other command is one route

alternatives: A separate boot module outside the CLI: rejected, it would be a new unit no spec establishes.
installShutdownSignalHandler alone: rejected, it knows nothing about the API server and would leave it serving through the daemon's own teardown.
payload.decision: The command group gains a fourth daemon verb, run, which composes createProductionDaemonDeps, Daemon.start() (spec 021 B-2's lock, journals, recovery, loop) and createApiServer (spec 022) in one foreground process. daemon start spawns exactly that verb detached, with the log at data/orchestrator/daemon.log. Shutdown is composed here rather than through installShutdownSignalHandler: SIGTERM or SIGINT stops the HTTP server first, then calls the daemon's own shutdown(), so the interface is gone before the identity lock is released.
payload.rationale: B-2 names start, stop and status, but nothing in the repository composed a daemon with its API, so those three verbs would have had no process to manage. Spec 021 owns daemon.ts and spec 022 owns the server, so the composition belongs to the one territory that may import both. Stopping the server before releasing the lock keeps the window where a client can reach a daemon that has already let go of its journals closed.
payload.title: daemon run is the foreground boot that daemon start spawns

alternatives: Add a journal accessor to daemon.ts: rejected here, it changes a unit spec 021 owns.
Open a second JournalHandle read-only: impossible, openJournal takes an exclusive per-chain lock the daemon already holds.
Reach into the Daemon's private fields through a cast: rejected, it would depend on a name no contract promises.
payload.decision: daemon run hands the API a read-only view built by journalViewFromDir(dir, basename) instead of journalViewFromHandle: it reads journal.jsonl and decisions.jsonl directly, re-parsing only when the file's size or mtime changes, and stopping at the first line that does not parse or does not continue the sequence, which is the torn tail journal.ts's own open-time recovery drops too. It is the only place in this territory that touches journal bytes; every fold still happens in the API's own read models.
payload.rationale: Spec 022 D-7 hands the API a view over the daemon's live handle, but that handle is a private field of the Daemon class, and spec 011's per-chain lock refuses a second writer, so an in-process API cannot obtain either one. Reading the append-only file is the honest alternative: it can only report records the daemon has already fsynced, which is exactly what a view over the handle would report, and it cannot append, lock, or race the writer. The alternative that would have been cleaner (a read accessor on Daemon) sits in spec 021's territory and would have required either amending a shipped kernel spec or a coupling waiver.
payload.title: The hosted API reads both chains from their files, not from the daemon's handle

alternatives: malformed-response as exit 2: rejected, it would hide a daemon that is running and broken behind the code for one that is absent.
daemon status always exiting 0: rejected, the answer would only be readable by parsing prose.
payload.decision: Only the unreachable error kind maps to exit 2; every other kind the API or the client can produce, malformed-response included, is an operational failure and exits 1. Usage errors (no command, unknown command, unknown flag, a flag missing its value, an unknown verb, a trailing argument) print the reason and the usage block to stderr and exit 3. daemon status also exits 2 when no live lock holder exists, so one code answers 'there is no daemon' whether the question went over HTTP or to the lock file.
payload.rationale: B-3 fixes the four codes but not which failures fall where. unreachable is the one kind api-client.ts produces without reaching the daemon, so it is the only honest 2; malformed-response means the daemon did answer, just not in the contract, which is an operational failure like a refused control. Giving daemon status the same 2 lets a script test one code before deciding whether to start a daemon.
payload.title: Exit 2 means there is no daemon, whichever command asked

alternatives: Map a broken chain to {ok:false,error:{kind:'conflict'}}: rejected, it overloads a server-side token with a local meaning.
A separate output shape for offline commands: rejected, clients would need two parsers for one binary.
payload.decision: journal verify and the daemon lifecycle verbs print {ok:true,data:{...}} under --json even when what they inspected is broken or absent: the verdict lives in data (verified, chains[].verified, running, staleLock, ready) and the outcome lives in the exit code. A tampered chain is {ok:true,data:{verified:false,...}} with exit 1; a missing anchor is reported the same way rather than thrown.
payload.rationale: The envelope's error kinds are the API's vocabulary for what a request did, and no request was made here. Borrowing conflict or internal for a broken hash chain would put a token in the stream that no server could ever have produced, and would make the CLI's own failures indistinguishable from the daemon's. Keeping ok:true says what is true: the command ran and produced an answer, and the answer is bad news.
payload.title: Offline commands answer ok:true with the verdict inside data

alternatives: Separate --host/--port for the daemon: rejected, it lets the bind address and the client address disagree silently.
Ignore unknown flags, as the observatory commands do: rejected, that defect is recorded in spec 005, not blessed.
payload.decision: A single --url base address tells a client where to look and tells daemon run|start where to bind (host and port are parsed out of it), resolved as --url, then OBSERVATORY_ORCHESTRATOR_URL, then http://127.0.0.1:4519. --data-dir and --repo override the orchestrator data directory and the target repository. Any other --flag, a valued flag with no value, and any unexpected positional argument are usage errors on stderr with exit 3.
payload.rationale: Two separate knobs (a bind port and a client url) is exactly how an operator ends up starting a daemon on one port and querying another without an error anywhere. Refusing unknown flags declines to inherit spec 005's recorded defect: silently swallowing a mistyped flag is cosmetic in a query command and dangerous in a control plane whose verbs journal irreversible facts, where --jsonn would have quietly executed the verb in human mode.
payload.title: One --url for both halves, and unknown flags are refused

alternatives: Only the API spellings: rejected, B-2 names skip|retry|reverify|force-gate|approve.
Leave the source at its default: rejected, provenance is the whole point of journaling a control with its source (spec 021 B-4).
payload.decision: spec <id> retry maps to the retry-stage route and spec <id> force-gate maps to force-human-gate, the API's own spellings being accepted as well, so B-2's grammar and spec 022 B-5's routes are the same set of verbs under two names. Every control the CLI issues carries X-Control-Source: cli, so the control record the daemon journals names the terminal, not the API.
payload.rationale: B-2 writes the verbs in their short form and spec 022 B-5 writes the routes in their long form; treating one as an alias of the other keeps both specs literally true without either surface renaming the other. Sourcing controls as cli is what makes the decision ledger and the journal able to answer who did this: without it every action taken from a terminal would be indistinguishable from one taken in the web UI, since both default to api.
payload.title: The CLI's spec verbs are aliases over the API's, and every control is sourced cli

alternatives: Serve the SPA from a second port or process, which would add an origin to trust and a CORS story spec 022 B-1 deliberately does not have.
Embed the built assets in the binary, which Bun supports but which would make `bun run web:build` a prerequisite of every typecheck rather than of the UI alone.
Fall back to index.html for every unmatched path, which is the common SPA default and which hides missing-asset bugs.
payload.decision: createStaticHandler answers GET and HEAD only, and returns null (leaving the API router to answer) for anything it is not certain about. It refuses the /api namespace before resolving anything from disk, so a built asset can never shadow a route and an unknown API path keeps leaving through spec 022 B-2's envelope rather than being handed an HTML page. Paths are resolved inside the build directory and the containment check is on the resolved absolute path, so percent-encoded or literal .. segments cannot escape. A path that names a file extension and misses is a genuine 404; a path without one is treated as a client-side route and gets index.html. Hashed assets under /assets/ are served immutable for a year and index.html is served no-store. A checkout whose UI was never built answers 503 with an HTML page naming `bun run web:build` and pointing at /api/meta to show the API is unaffected. The server dep is `staticDir`, where omitted means the checkout's own web/dist and null disables static serving entirely.
payload.rationale: Spec 024 B-1 fixes the origin but not the resolution rules, and each of these is a way the UI could quietly corrupt the API's contract. Falling back to the shell for a missing /assets/*.js would turn a bad bundle reference into an inscrutable syntax error in the console instead of a 404. Serving index.html with a cache would keep a rebuilt UI on the previous bundle. Answering /api from disk would let a file shadow a route. A blank page for an unbuilt UI reads as a broken daemon when the API beside it is healthy, which is exactly the dishonesty B-7 rules out.
payload.title: The static handler refuses /api first and falls back to the shell only for extensionless paths

alternatives: Clear all state on a failed fetch, which is honest about liveness but throws away the last known truth and makes a transient blip look like a cold start.
Leave the last fold on screen with no banner, which is the stale-but-live-looking dashboard AC-2 names as the failure.
Treat any single route failure as unreachable, which would misreport a disagreeing but healthy daemon as dead.
payload.decision: The store tracks `reach` as unknown, reachable, or unreachable. A refresh folds the five read routes together and claims unreachable only when every one of them failed with the client's own `unreachable` error kind: a daemon that answered even one route with an error is up and disagreeing, which is a different fact and is shown as that route's error instead. A failed refetch keeps the previous data and its `loadedAtMs` and adds the error, because dropping the data would hide what was true and dropping the error would make stale data look live. While nothing is streaming, a 4 s /api/meta probe is what turns a killed daemon into an explicit unreachable state; when the probe finds the daemon again it triggers a full refold rather than letting the pre-death values stand. The App renders this as a banner naming the state and the base url with how long ago contact was last made, and marks every panel stale.
payload.rationale: AC-2 requires that killing the daemon degrade to an explicit unreachable state rather than a stale-but-live-looking dashboard, and the honest version of that is not a blank screen. The last fold the daemon confirmed is genuinely the last thing known to be true, so it is kept; what must not happen is for it to look current. Distinguishing 'nothing got through' from 'the daemon answered with an error' matters because collapsing them would report a healthy daemon as dead the moment one route disagreed.
payload.title: Unreachable is claimed only when nothing got through, and the last good fold is kept but marked stale

alternatives: Ask the daemon for a dry-run preview, which would need a new API surface spec 022 does not have and a second round trip before every confirmation.
Preview only the verb name without the payload, which is honest but does not satisfy B-6's 'exact control record'.
Disable controls the plan says will be refused, which trades a wrong-looking button for an unreachable one.
payload.decision: planControl is a pure function of the verb, its target, and the run state the API last served. It classifies every control into one of three effects: `journals` (with the exact kind and payload, including the `web-ui` source the client sends), `no-op` (spec 022 B-5's idempotent case, previewed as 'No record will be journaled.' rather than as a record that will not exist), and `refused` (previewed with the daemon's own reason). Start on a paused run previews a control.resume, because spec 022 D-1 makes that the record that actually lands. A plan whose effect is `refused` still renders a confirm button reading 'Send anyway': the plan is a prediction from the last fetched state and the daemon is the one that decides, so the UI does not disable a control on the strength of its own stale guess. Nothing is issued until the confirmation is accepted, and after it the surrounding views refold from the read routes rather than being patched from the control's answer.
payload.rationale: B-6 requires that each control show the exact record that will be journaled before confirming, which forces the UI to model the daemon's own guards. Two failure modes follow, and both are worse than not previewing. Showing a record for an idempotent no-op would promise a journal entry that never appears. Disabling a refused verb would let a stale run status make a control unreachable even after the daemon moved on, which is the optimistic UI B-7 forbids pointed the other way.
payload.title: The confirmation previews a computed plan, and a verb the daemon will refuse is labelled but still sendable

alternatives: Generate a client into web/ from the route table at build time, which adds a codegen step and a generated artifact to review for a contract that is already shared source.
Declare the response shapes locally in web/, which decouples the build at the cost of exactly the drift D-8 was written to prevent.
payload.decision: web/src/api.ts is a re-export seam over src/orchestrator/api/types.ts and src/orchestrator/api/api-client.ts, and it is the only module in web/ that reaches outside web/. The SPA therefore takes every path from API_ROUTES and every payload shape from types.ts, so a route or a shape cannot drift between the daemon and this client without failing typecheck. The base url is always window.location.origin, so there is no configuration to get wrong and no second origin to trust, and every control this UI issues carries the source `web-ui`. The two imported modules are pure of Node built-ins, which is what keeps the bundle a browser bundle despite importing from src/.
payload.rationale: Spec 022 D-8 made api-client.ts route-table driven precisely so that a hand-written client could not drift from the server, and named the web UI as one of the two clients that promise buys. Re-declaring the wire shapes inside web/ would have thrown that away on the first day and turned every future API change into a silent two-sided edit. Typecheck now fails on the drift instead.
payload.title: The SPA imports the API territory's own types and client rather than declaring a second copy

alternatives: Use @testing-library/react, which is the conventional choice and adds a dependency tree for three operations.
Register happy-dom once at module scope, which is simpler and silently breaks the real-HTTP tests elsewhere in the suite.
Run the web tests in a separate bun test invocation with its own preload, which isolates the globals at the cost of splitting the gate's `bun test` into two commands.
payload.decision: The component tests run under `bun test` with a hand-rolled harness (mount, click, read by data-testid, all through React's own act) rather than a testing library, since those three operations are all the tests need. happy-dom is registered in a beforeAll and unregistered in an afterAll rather than as a module-level side effect, because bun test runs every file in one process and the registrator replaces 35 globals that Bun owns, including fetch, Response, and Request; leaving them replaced breaks the API territory's own route tests, which serve real HTTP over a real Bun.serve in the same run. The end-to-end file additionally captures Bun's HTTP globals before registration and puts them back after it, so a real client and a real Bun.serve can meet under a real DOM.
payload.rationale: FR-002 asks for component tests, and spec 024 B-1's no-external-anything posture is easier to keep honest with a short dependency list. The global-registration scoping is not a style preference: it is the difference between this territory's tests passing and the API territory's tests failing, in a suite that shares one process. The end-to-end file needs both halves at once, which neither the registered nor the unregistered state provides on its own.
payload.title: happy-dom is registered per test file and the render harness is hand-rolled, with the end-to-end file restoring Bun's HTTP globals

alternatives: Add a client router such as react-router, which brings a dependency and a history API for five tabs.
Render state directly from event payloads, which is faster and is the optimistic UI B-7 forbids.
Tick the countdown against the browser clock, which needs no skew tracking and drifts against the daemon.
payload.decision: The five views (run, dag, quota, decisions, history) are selected by window.location.hash with no router dependency, defaulting to run for an unrecognised fragment. The SSE tail is bounded at 400 events, which is a window on the stream rather than a transcript, since the full history lives in the journal the read routes serve. Events are never a source of truth: an event triggers a refetch, debounced at 400 ms so a busy build does not refold the DAG once per streamed line, and the rendered values always come from the read routes. Reconnection is left to EventSource's own Last-Event-ID replay against spec 022 B-4's ring, with a full refold on reconnect because the ring is bounded and a long outage drops records. The quota countdown is the one number the page computes rather than reads, so it counts against the daemon's clock, reconstructed from the skew between /api/quota's `nowMs` and the page's clock when that response arrived, and the `estimated` flag is always rendered alongside it.
payload.rationale: B-3 asks for a scrollback-bounded tail and B-7 forbids optimistic UI, which together mean the stream can drive refetches but must not drive state. Counting the quota timer against the browser's clock would drift against the thing actually holding the timer, and a countdown that hides an inferred horizon is exactly the confident-looking number this spec's purpose section rules out. Hash routing keeps the SPA a single static file with no server-side route table, which is what lets static.ts fall back to the shell without knowing the view names.
payload.title: Hash routing over five views, a 400-event scrollback with debounced refetch, and a countdown ticked against the daemon's clock

alternatives: Copy the target to a temp tree and compile the copy: unbounded cost per qualification, and a compile of a copy is not the check B-4 names.
Skip the compile check and infer greenness from committed .derived/ artifacts: that reads compiled JSON directly, which governed-artifact-reads.md forbids, and it would trust stale output.
Snapshot and restore .derived/ around the compile: hides a real staleness signal and writes twice instead of once.
payload.decision: qualifyProject() runs `spec-spine compile` with the target as cwd, exactly as B-4 requires, accepting that compile rewrites that repo's own .derived/ tree. Every other probe call (git rev-parse, remote get-url, symbolic-ref, check-ignore, and the specs/ read) is strictly read-only. The module header and the probe's doc comment state this explicitly so the exception is recorded rather than discovered.
payload.rationale: B-4 mandates a compile-green check and B-5 says the orchestrator writes nothing in a target outside its state root; the two collide because spec-spine has no check-only compile mode (`spec-spine compile --help` offers only --repo). B-4's own closing sentence draws the line that resolves it: the orchestrator never edits a target's authored files. .derived/ is deterministic output of the corpus, not an authored file, and recompiling it is idempotent when the corpus is green, which is precisely the condition the check is asserting.
payload.title: Qualification's spec-spine compile is the one write inside a target, and it touches only derived artifacts

alternatives: Fall back to the local HEAD branch when origin has no refs: turns the check into a tautology and can hand the build stage a feature branch as its base.
Query the remote over the network (git ls-remote --symref): makes qualification depend on network reachability and credentials, which is not what B-4 asks about.
payload.decision: ProjectProbe.defaultBranch() resolves `git symbolic-ref --short refs/remotes/origin/HEAD` first, falls back to verifying refs/remotes/origin/main and then refs/remotes/origin/master, and returns null otherwise. The locally checked-out branch is never used as a fallback, and the failing check's detail names all three refs it tried.
payload.rationale: B-4 asks for a resolvable default branch as part of a git-repo-with-origin check, so the branch it means is the one pull requests merge into: an origin property. Falling back to `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` would make the check pass for any repo with a commit, including a target sitting on a leftover feature branch, and the build stage would then normalize onto the wrong base (spec 018's own preflight lesson).
payload.title: A resolvable default branch means refs/remotes/origin/HEAD, then origin/main, then origin/master, and nothing else

alternatives: Accept a subdirectory and silently register its work-tree root instead: registers something the operator did not ask for.
Allow several names per repoDir for different profiles: profiles do not exist, and the collision is on shared mutable state, not on naming.
payload.decision: The git-repo check passes only when `git rev-parse --show-prefix` returns the empty string (repoDir is the work tree root); a path inside a repo fails with the prefix quoted in its reason. registerProject() additionally refuses a repoDir already registered under another live name, alongside D-1's name uniqueness.
payload.rationale: Both rules protect the state root. A subdirectory registration would put data/orchestrator/ somewhere inside the repo while every git operation acted on the parent, and two names for one repoDir would give two projects one state root: two folds of the same journals, one writer lock contended between them, and spec 026's scheduler driving the same checkout twice in a pass. D-1 makes the name the registry's key but says nothing about the path, so the path rule is recorded here.
payload.title: A target must be a work-tree root, and one repoDir may back only one live project

alternatives: Stamp checkedAt inside the verdict at qualification time: two clocks for one event, and a verdict computed but journaled later would lie about when it was recorded.
Expose only the raw payload and let each caller find the timestamp: pushes the same join into the API, the CLI, and the UI.
payload.decision: QualificationVerdict (what qualifyProject returns and what a register/requalify payload stores) is {qualified, checks, warnings}. The folded Project exposes RecordedQualification, the same verdict plus checkedAt taken from the journal record's own ts. Mutations return {record, project} so a control surface can render either the journaled record or the resulting project.
payload.rationale: B-1 calls qualification 'the latest recorded verdict', and the chain already timestamps every record. A checkedAt inside the payload would be a second clock that could disagree with the envelope's, and it would make two byte-different payloads out of one identical verdict, which weakens any later content-hash comparison of verdicts.
payload.title: A qualification verdict carries no clock of its own; the fold stamps checkedAt from the recording record

alternatives: Throw on a record naming an unknown project: one stale line takes down every project's registry read.
Re-create the project from the mutation record: invents a repoDir and a verdict that nobody recorded.
payload.decision: foldProjects() applies arm, disarm, and requalify records only when the named project is currently live; a record naming a removed (or never registered) project changes nothing, and only a fresh registration brings a name back. Record kinds outside the five project.* kinds are skipped. Malformed payloads of an owned kind still throw a typed error.
payload.rationale: D-2 makes removal a tombstone on an append-only chain, so a control that raced the removal (or landed just before a crash) must not resurrect the project and hand spec 026's scheduler a target the operator had already withdrawn. Ignoring is the correct semantics here rather than leniency; throwing instead would make one stale line render the whole registry unreadable, which is the opposite of B-4's 'stay visible with reasons' stance.
payload.title: A mutation record naming a project that is not live is inert in the fold, and foreign kinds are ignored

alternatives: Call git and fs directly inside qualifyProject: no seam, and every FR-002 fixture would then need a real compilable corpus.
Count any entry under specs/: a directory of notes with no spec.md would qualify a target the scheduler cannot use.
payload.decision: Every fact qualification needs (git prefix, origin url, default branch, compile result, spec count, data/ ignored) sits behind the injected ProjectProbe; createProcessProjectProbe() is the production implementation and qualifyProject() is the assembler that owns the reason wording. The specs-present check counts directories under specs/ that hold a spec.md, reporting the count, rather than counting raw directory entries. Tests run the production probe against real git fixture directories with only compile() scripted.
payload.rationale: The seam matches the convention every other kernel module already follows (dag.ts's DagReader, the stage modules' Runner), and it is what lets FR-002's fixtures be genuine repositories without any of them needing a governed corpus and an installed spec-spine. Counting spec.md files rather than bare entries satisfies B-4's 'exists and is non-empty' with the stricter reading: a specs/ directory holding no spec is nothing for the DAG to schedule, and the count itself is a useful reason string.
payload.title: Qualification facts come through an injected ProjectProbe, and specs-present counts specs/*/spec.md

alternatives: Run the full 025 preflight on every scan
Requalify on a slower second interval
Never re-read anything and wake only on an explicit control
payload.decision: B-4's 'requalifies cheaply' is one governed registry read per qualified project per scan (loadRegistrySnapshot through that project's injected DagReader), plus the recorded 025 verdict. The scan never re-runs qualifyProject: an unqualified project is skipped on its recorded verdict alone with the failing checks reported, and a read that throws marks the project 'unreadable' with the message rather than rewriting any verdict. Full requalification stays an explicit operator action through 025's requalifyProject, surfaced by 027 and 028.
payload.rationale: qualifyProject runs spec-spine compile inside the target (025 D-1): the one write the registry ever makes there, and seconds of work per project. Doing that every 60 s across every registered project would turn an idle daemon into a background compile loop writing into repositories nobody asked it to touch, and would silently flip a project's armed-and-qualified state on a transient failure. The registry read is the fact the scan actually needs, since B-4's job is noticing newly pending work.
payload.title: The standby scan requalifies by reading a target's registry, never by re-running the preflight

alternatives: Re-drive on every scan whenever anything is pending
Journal the signature into a chain so restarts inherit it
Key the signature on the pending set alone (misses a dependency completing)
payload.decision: When a project's run reaches a terminal status the scheduler records the registry signature it concluded on: every spec id paired with its implementation field, sorted and joined. That project is skipped on later scans while its signature is unchanged, and any flip (a spec becoming pending, a spec completing, a spec appearing) wakes a fresh run. The signature is in-memory only, so a daemon restart re-evaluates every project once.
payload.rationale: Without it, a project holding a pending spec that is permanently blocked would get a brand new run every scan interval, each journaling run.created, run.blocked, and a terminal transition into that project's chain forever. B-4 asks for newly ready work to wake a run, which is a change detector, not a poll; the signature is the cheapest honest one over facts the scan already read. Keeping it in memory rather than journaling it means a restart cannot inherit a stale conclusion, at the cost of one no-op run per project per restart, which 021 D-12 already treats as normal.
payload.title: A concluded project is not re-driven until its own registry says something new

alternatives: Leave the registry empty until spec 028 ships a projects command
Re-register whenever the fold is empty
Treat the self-hosted checkout as an implicit project outside the registry
payload.decision: StandbyDeps takes an optional bootstrap {repoDir, probe}. When the projects chain holds zero records, the scheduler qualifies that repoDir through 025's qualifyProject and registers it (source cli, armed by default). The test is the chain's own emptiness, not the fold's: once anything has ever been registered the bootstrap never fires again, so a registry an operator emptied stays empty. A registration that throws is logged and the daemon still boots into standby.
payload.rationale: 025 registers projects but ships no surface for adding one; that arrives with 028. Without a bootstrap, daemon run on a fresh checkout would hold a lock, serve an API, and drive nothing, which is a worse version of the failure 010 A-1 is about. 025 already says the self-hosted checkout is simply the first registered project and 010 D14 says pointing the orchestrator at a project is the consent, so adopting the checkout --repo names is the reading both decisions already imply. Gating on a virgin chain rather than an empty fold keeps a deliberate removal from being undone on the next boot.
payload.title: A registry chain that has never held a record adopts the daemon's own --repo as its first project

alternatives: Append standby.* kinds to the projects chain
Open a fourth hash-linked chain for standby
Expose nothing and let 027 recompute it
payload.decision: Standby journals nothing durable. Each project's run keeps writing its own chains inside its own state root (011, 013, 021 unchanged), the registry chain stays 025's, and what the scheduler knows on top of those (which project holds the flight slot, what the last scan saw, why a project is not being driven) is exposed as a StandbySnapshot and written to the daemon home's log through an injected log seam. B-4's 'reported' is that snapshot plus that log; specs 027 and 029 render it.
payload.rationale: The two candidates were appending standby.* kinds to 025's registry chain, which would mix scheduler telemetry into the chain that answers what may this daemon touch, or opening a fourth chain in the daemon home, which no verify surface covers (journal verify walks work and decisions; 028 is where the registry joins it). Neither earns its keep, because everything standby knows is a fact about right now that the next scan replaces: it is state, not history, and this repository's chains are for history. B-6 already names the log as living in the daemon home.
payload.title: The scheduler opens no chain of its own; what it observes is a snapshot and a log line

alternatives: Leave controls unattached until 027
Always forward to the self-hosted project
Pick the first registered project when ambiguous
payload.decision: daemon run hands the API a ControlTarget that forwards every 021 B-4 verb to the daemon holding the flight slot; in standby it forwards to the single live paused run when there is exactly one. No live run throws 'the daemon is in standby', and two or more throws with the candidate project names listed. runControl turns both into a conflict envelope, so no control is ever applied to a project the caller did not name.
payload.rationale: 022's routes were written when one daemon meant one run, and 026 puts API surface out of scope precisely because 027 replaces them with project-scoped routes. The choice was between leaving the routes wired to nothing (breaking the working CLI and UI for the common single-project case) and guessing a project when several are live. Forwarding to the unambiguous target and refusing loudly otherwise keeps today's surface working without inventing a routing rule 027 would have to undo.
payload.title: Spec 022's control routes address the flight-slot holder, and refuse when the target is ambiguous

alternatives: Let each supervised daemon reclaim its own project's locks
Clear every project lock on every boot
Never clear and require manual removal after a kill
payload.decision: A supervised Daemon takes no identity lock and performs no lock reclaim. The scheduler does both: acquireDaemonLock over the daemon home, and, only when that returned a reclaim (the previous daemon proven dead by pid plus process start time), it clears projects.lock in the daemon home before opening the registry and then journal.lock and decisions.lock in every registered project's state root. daemon.lock is never in that set. Without a reclaim nothing is cleared, so a target whose journals are held by a live writer is reported and retried on the next scan rather than forced. forceReleaseStandbyLocks exports the same sweep for an outside supervisor.
payload.rationale: 021 B-1's identity check is strictly stronger than spec 011's file-existence lock, so a reclaim is the one moment a supervisor can honestly conclude that every chain lock the dead daemon could have been holding is stale, and B-6 says the projects it may have been writing are exactly the registered ones. Clearing unconditionally would let a second daemon in a second checkout stomp a live writer; clearing nothing would leave a killed daemon's projects unopenable with no path back but manual surgery. 011 section 6 deliberately leaves this to a supervisor, and the standby daemon is the first thing in this repository that actually is one.
payload.title: Stale per-chain locks are cleared by the supervisor, only on a proven reclaim

alternatives: Require an explicit pick before anything renders: honest, but it makes a single-project daemon click through a menu for the only answer there is.
Always follow the daemon's active project with no operator override: unusable for inspecting a project the daemon is not currently driving.
Keep a per-project cache of folds in the store: more state to invalidate, and the read routes are cheap enough that a refold on switch is simpler and cannot go stale.
payload.decision: The v2 break retires the unscoped read routes, so the SPA can no longer fetch a DAG without naming a project. The store holds one selected project and reads dag, run, history, and decisions through client.project(name); meta, quota, and the event stream stay global. The selection resolves in this order: a selection the operator made, for as long as the registry still carries it; otherwise the daemon's own activeProject from /api/meta; otherwise the registry's first row; otherwise null. A change of selection drops the previous project's folds rather than letting them stand under the new name, and with no project selected the scoped panels render empty and the decision form refuses to search. The header carries the picker, so the project every panel is showing is always named on screen.
payload.rationale: Spec 027 governs the wire and is silent on the UI, but retiring v1 forces the question: something has to choose the project, and the honest options are to ask the operator or to follow the daemon. Following the daemon's activeProject first means the dashboard opens on the project actually being driven, which is what an operator watching a build wants; falling through to the first row means a single-project daemon (the common case) needs no choosing at all. Carrying a previous project's fold across a switch would be exactly the misstatement of scope B-6 asks the API to prevent, so the folds are dropped instead of reused. Keeping the selection through a failed registry read stops a transient error from swapping the view out from under the operator. Scope note: spec 029 owns the real project switcher, the registry controls, and the standby view. What landed here is only the minimum that keeps the corpus green across the break, because the SPA imports the client directly and could neither typecheck nor fetch a DAG without naming a project. No registry mutation is offered from the UI, which is 029's to give.
payload.title: The web UI resolves one selected project and scopes every panel through it

alternatives: Keep one flat client and pass the project as the first argument to every scoped method: compiles, but every call site becomes a place to pass the wrong name, and nothing stops a component from addressing a project the shell is not showing.
Generate the client from the route table at build time: spec 022 D-8 already rejected code generation for this surface, and the break gave no new reason to revisit it.
payload.decision: createApiClient returns the global half (meta, quota, projects, the registry controls, eventsUrl) plus client.project(name), which returns a ProjectClient carrying every scoped read and control with the project name fixed at construction rather than passed per call. The route table splits the same way: API_ROUTES holds the whole global paths, PROJECT_ROUTES holds the scoped suffixes, and projectRoute(project, suffix) is the one place a scoped URL is built. No v1 path survives in either table.
payload.rationale: Spec 022 D-8 made the client route-table driven so a path cannot drift between server and client without failing typecheck; v2 has to keep that promise across a break that moves most routes. Fixing the project name when the sub-client is made, rather than threading it through every call, means a caller cannot mix two projects in one sequence of calls by accident, and a caller that has not decided which project it means has no unscoped dag() to reach for. The split table mirrors the split router, so both halves of a scoped path are checked by the compiler.
payload.title: The typed client splits into a global half and a per-project sub-client

alternatives: Fold every project's DAG inside the global refresh: simpler, but it puts N spec-spine invocations on the event-burst path.
Serve a fleet-wide backlog route from the daemon: that is orchestration behavior the API territory owns, and spec 029 is explicitly out of scope for it.
payload.decision: The store keeps one DAG fold per registered project in its own map, refolded by an explicit refreshBacklogs() action that the shell calls when the standby view is open and when the registry's names change, rather than as part of the global refresh. Every row renders the moment its own fold was confirmed, and a project absent from the map renders as not folded rather than as an empty backlog.
payload.rationale: A DAG fold runs spec-spine inside the target repository. Folding the whole registry on every event burst would multiply that cost by the number of registered projects several times a second, for a view that is usually not on screen. Spec 029 B-2 requires the summaries to exist and to be honest, not to be continuously live, so the honest thing is to read them when the view asks and to render the age of each fold.
payload.title: The standby view's per-project backlogs are read on demand, not with every refresh

alternatives: Subscribe with ?project=<selected> and reopen the stream on every switch: it drops the cross-project refetch trigger and pays a reconnect and replay per project switch.
payload.decision: The SPA subscribes to /api/events without a ?project= predicate and applies the selected project's filter when rendering the live tail, using the same predicate the server implements (a daemon-scoped event belongs to every project's tail). Last-Event-ID replay is unchanged.
payload.rationale: Spec 029 B-5 requires the tail to be filtered to the selected project, and it does not say where the filter runs. One stream is also this page's refetch trigger: filtering server-side would leave the switcher's rows and the standby view's backlogs refreshing only on the liveness probe, because another project's activity would never reach the client. Filtering at render satisfies B-5 while keeping every project's row live.
payload.title: The event subscription stays unfiltered; the selected project's filter is applied to what is rendered

alternatives: Key the control by verb so a flip remounts it: the answer would vanish the instant it arrived.
Hold the row's pre-call armed state in the panel: it spreads one control's state across the view that renders it.
payload.decision: RegistryControlButton captures its verb when the dialog opens and uses that captured verb for the preview, the label, the call it issues, and its test id, releasing it on dismiss. The verb prop is only read while the control sits idle.
payload.rationale: The standby row offers arm or disarm depending on the registry's own armed flag, so confirming an arm flips the prop the moment the refold lands (024 B-7 refolds rather than patching locally). A dialog reading the prop would then re-label itself Disarm over the arm record it just journaled, which is the confirmation pattern reporting a request the operator never made. Freezing the verb keeps 024 B-6's promise exact: what is shown after confirming is the answer to what was confirmed.
payload.title: An open registry dialog keeps the verb it was opened with until it is dismissed

alternatives: No opt-out: strictly one project's lines. Simpler, and it makes the daemon's own cross-project activity invisible from the only view that streams.
Filter the subscription server-side per project: rejected in 029-d2-unfiltered-stream for a separate reason, and it would make the opt-out a reconnect.
payload.decision: The run panel's tail applies the selected project's filter by default and offers an "every project" checkbox that widens it to the whole stream. The counter states how many of the buffered records are being shown, so a widened tail is never mistaken for the scoped one.
payload.rationale: Spec 029 B-5 requires the tail to be filtered to the selected project, which is what the default does; it does not say whether the operator may look at the whole stream. One daemon drives many projects from one flight slot, and an operator watching a handover has a real reason to see both chains at once. The honesty rule is satisfied by labelling which view is on rather than by removing the wider one: an unlabelled mixed tail would be the scope error, not the mixing itself.
payload.title: The live tail filters to the selected project by default, with a labelled opt-out

alternatives: Add an `armed` field to POST /api/projects: correct long-term, but it edits spec 027's unit from spec 028's session.
Print only the disarm envelope: loses the registration record, which is the one an operator most needs to see.
Roll the registration back when the disarm fails: the CLI would be issuing a removal nobody asked for, against an append-only chain.
payload.decision: `projects add <path> --disarmed` issues POST /api/projects to register the project (armed, per 010 D14) and then POST /api/projects/<name>/disarm against the name the chain journaled. Human output prints both journaled records; `--json` prints {ok: true, data: {registered, disarmed}} composed from the two served payloads, and without the flag the single served envelope is printed verbatim. A registration that lands followed by a disarm that fails prints the served failure, exits 1, and states on stderr that the project is registered and still armed.
payload.rationale: v2's registration route carries no `armed` field, and the API is spec 027's territory: widening it from a CLI build session would take a unit this spec does not own. Two controls against routes that already exist keep the client a client, and the composed `--json` payload is exactly 023 D-1's rule (compose served payloads, declare no new shape). Half-applied and saying so beats a compensating removal this client has no authority to perform.
payload.title: projects add --disarmed is register then disarm, not one route

alternatives: Send the path verbatim and let the registry refuse it: correct but useless, since `projects add .` is the natural way to register the repo you are standing in.
Resolve it server-side against the daemon's cwd: silently registers a different directory whenever the two processes differ.
payload.decision: `projects add <path>` resolves the path against the CLI process's working directory before sending it, so the registry always receives an absolute path the operator can recognise.
payload.rationale: Spec 025's normalizeRepoDir refuses a relative repoDir outright, and the daemon's working directory is not the operator's, so a relative path resolved server-side would name a different repository than the one typed in front of it. Resolving where the shell is is the only reading that cannot silently register the wrong checkout.
payload.title: projects add resolves its path against the invoking shell

alternatives: Throw and let the dispatcher's catch print it: loses the envelope under `--json` and gives a bare stderr line where D-5 promises a document.
Answer with an API error kind (`not-found`): borrows a vocabulary for requests when no request was made.
payload.decision: The offline verify envelope gains `project` (which registry entry the state root came from, null for `--dir` and for the self-hosted default) and `resolveError`. A `--project` the registry does not hold answers {ok: true, data: {verified: false, resolveError, chains: []}} with exit 1, and prints the reason on stderr in human mode.
payload.rationale: Spec 023 D-5 already fixes the shape for offline commands: the verdict lives inside `data`, the outcome lives in the exit code, and the API's error kinds are not borrowed because no request was made. An unresolved project is the same class of fact as a broken chain, so it takes the same shape rather than a second convention. The registry fold is a file read of the daemon home's projects chain, never an API call, which is what keeps 023 B-4's independent check independent.
payload.title: journal verify reports an unresolvable --project in its own envelope

alternatives: Always require --project: safe, but makes the single-project case (the self-hosted one, and everything specs 010-024 shipped against) worse for nothing.
Pre-check the name against GET /api/projects before scoping: an extra round trip that turns the daemon's own not-found into a second, less precise one.
payload.decision: The verbs B-2 scopes (dag, next, start, pause, resume, history, decisions, the spec verbs, and `status --project`) resolve the sole registered project when `--project` is absent, refuse with a `conflict` naming every candidate (exit 1) when the daemon holds several, and refuse with `not-found` when it holds none. `--project <name>` is passed to the route as given: an unknown name comes back not-found from the daemon, which is B-4's operational failure and not something the client pre-empts by listing the registry first.
payload.rationale: One registered project is the overwhelmingly common case and typing its name every time would be friction for no safety. Several is different: these verbs journal irreversible controls, so picking one out of a set nobody named would act on a repository the operator never addressed. Naming the candidates in the refusal makes the fix the next thing they can type.
payload.title: Without --project a scoped verb takes the sole project or refuses by name

alternatives: Ignore inapplicable flags: reintroduces the exact defect spec 005 recorded and 023 D-6 refused.
Make every flag global in meaning: there is no coherent meaning for `--disarmed` on `projects remove`.
payload.decision: Each command declares the extra flags it accepts (`--project` for the scoped verbs, `--project`/`--dir` for journal verify, `--name`/`--disarmed` for projects add, none for daemon and the rest of the projects group). A flag that parses but means nothing to the verb at hand exits 3 with the usage block, exactly as an unknown flag does. An unknown command is reported as an unknown command first, so a typo is not answered with a complaint about its flags.
payload.rationale: Spec 023 D-6 refuses `--jsonn` rather than ignoring it because silent flag-swallowing in a control plane whose verbs journal irreversible facts is worse than an annoyance. `--project alpha` on `daemon status`, or `--disarmed` on `projects arm`, is the same defect wearing a different hat: the operator asked for something the command will not do, and being told beats being ignored.
payload.title: A known flag that the verb cannot use is a usage error, like an unknown one

alternatives: One row per SpecExec: renders a retried spec as several partial rows and makes AC-2's row-per-shipped-spec reading ambiguous.
Totals with a summed wall-clock: adds a figure whose unit (overlapping? sequential?) the journal cannot say.
payload.decision: Rows are keyed by spec id, aggregating every SpecExec and stage attempt the journal holds for that spec. The whole-journal totals carry the run-level aggregates (sessions by termination kind, remediation rounds, hook blocks, cost, quota parks, parked duration) but no wall-clock field.
payload.rationale: AC-2 asks for a row for every spec the journal shows shipped and B-4 renders per-spec rows; a retried spec is one line of "what did this spec need", not one line per attempt. A wall-clock summed across runs measures nothing an operator can act on, so totals omit it rather than serve a number with no referent.
payload.title: "Per spec execution" folds to one row per spec id; totals ride without wall-clock

alternatives: Drop unattributable sessions entirely: makes the totals disagree with a grep over the journal, which is exactly the hand-fold this spec exists to replace.
Attribute by nearest stage record's specId: a second bookkeeping path that can only disagree with the SpecExec-based one under the same serial loop.
payload.decision: session.result records carry no specId (spec 014 journals them from inside the driver), so the fold replays the journal in order and credits each one to the SpecExec whose specexec.created record was most recent, and through it to that exec's run. A session with no SpecExec anywhere before it in the journal belongs to no spec and no run; the whole-journal totals still count it.
payload.rationale: This is historyView's own attribution rule, exact under the serial loop spec 021 B-3 guarantees (one spec walked at a time, a retry minting a fresh SpecExec before its stages run). Adding a specId to session records would be a write path, which spec 030 declares out of scope.
payload.title: A session.result is credited to the most recently created SpecExec

alternatives: Count hook-blocked session classifications: a duplicate of sessionsByTermination["hook-blocked"] under a second name.
payload.decision: hookBlockedStages counts StageExec entities whose folded status is "blocked", per spec and per run. Sessions that classified hook-blocked remain visible as their own bucket in the termination-kind map and are not double-counted into this field.
payload.rationale: "blocked" is the sink the daemon transitions a stage into exactly on a hook-blocked or refused stage outcome (daemon.ts's isBlockedOutcome edge), and FR-001's fixture list names "a hook-blocked stage", not a session. Counting the stage-level fact adds information the kind map does not already carry.
payload.title: "Hook-blocked outcomes" counts StageExecs folded to "blocked"

alternatives: Exclude post-park re-attempts by scanning for an interleaved quota.parked: cheaper to game than to trust, and no longer B-1's plain count.
payload.decision: remediationRounds counts every StageExec minted at attempt > 1, whatever forced the fresh attempt: a red-gate retry, a crash retry, and the re-attempt after a quota park all count.
payload.rationale: B-1's words are "stage attempts beyond the first counted as remediation rounds", and the retry bookkeeping is already exact in the entities (spec 013 B-4 mints a fresh StageExec at attempt+1). Inventing a taxonomy of why each retry happened would be a second classification layer a later spec can derive from these same records if it earns its keep.
payload.title: Remediation rounds are stage attempts beyond the first, verbatim

alternatives: Anchor at specexec.created: measures queue time the spec's own stages never spent.
First terminal wins: a re-verified spec would report a span its later work escaped.
payload.decision: A spec's wallClockMs spans the first state.transition.intent for any of its StageExecs to the last state.transition.outcome moving one of its SpecExecs into shipped or failed. A run's spans its first stage intent to the run's own completed/failed outcome. Either end missing, or an unparseable timestamp, makes the value null.
payload.rationale: B-1 names "first stage intent to terminal transition". SpecExec has no graph-sink terminal (013 D-2: shipped can invalidate, failed can retry), so shipped/failed, the states the pipeline actually stops at, are the honest reading; last-wins on the terminal end keeps remediation and re-verification inside the measured span.
payload.title: Wall-clock runs from the first stage intent to the last terminal transition

alternatives: Sum closed windows and ignore the open one: understates silently, which is the laundering B-2 exists to forbid.
Take nowMs as an argument: stops being the pure fold B-1 names, and every caller's clock would change the answer.
payload.decision: parkedMs sums quota.parked-to-quota.resumed windows, preferring the resume record's own resumedAtMs over its envelope timestamp. A park never resumed, or superseded by a second park before any resume, leaves the total null rather than a floor passed off as the whole; zero parks is an honest zero. Parks attribute to the run whose run.created record was most recent.
payload.rationale: The fold is pure over (records, project) (FR-001), so an open park's span would need a "now" the function does not have, and B-2 forbids serving the closed windows' sum as if it covered the open one. Zero parks is complete knowledge, not an absence, so it is 0 and not null.
payload.title: Parked duration sums closed park windows; an open park makes the total unknown

alternatives: Add economics to PROJECT_ROUTES and a ProjectClient method: touches types.ts and api-client.ts, units this spec does not extend.
payload.decision: ECONOMICS_ROUTE and the view types live in src/orchestrator/economics.ts; state.ts's assembly adds only generatedAt (the daemon's clock, FR-002); the CLI fetches the one route directly, building the path from the shared constants and mapping transport failure into the envelope exactly as the typed client does. api/types.ts's PROJECT_ROUTES and api-client.ts are untouched.
payload.rationale: Spec 030 extends only server.ts, state.ts, and commands/orchestrator.ts.
